titre: The Unions of 1884 Are Free, but Must Declare Themselves to the Mayor
accroche: On March 21, 1884, the Waldeck-Rousseau law authorizes trade unions, provided they file their bylaws at city hall.
contenu_vulgarise:
Paris, March 21, 1884. After more than three years of back-and-forth between the two chambers of Parliament, begun on November 22, 1880, when a bill was introduced in the Chamber of Deputies, President Jules Grévy signs the law on the creation of trade unions. The text, carried by Interior Minister Pierre Waldeck-Rousseau in Jules Ferry's government, ends ninety-three years of prohibition: its first article repeals the law of June 14-17, 1791, known as the Le Chapelier law, and Article 416 of the penal code that had carried it over.

## A Freedom You Must Declare

Article 2 of the law authorizes unions or professional associations to form freely, without government authorization, even when they bring together more than twenty people. The point matters: the general law of April 18, 1834 then required prior authorization for any association of more than twenty members, on pain of Articles 291 to 294 of the penal code. Trade unions are expressly exempted from this common rule, which explains why a special law was needed for them rather than a simple loosening of the general law on associations.

This freedom is not unconditional, however. Article 4 requires the founders of any union to file its bylaws and the names of its leaders at the town hall of the commune where it is established, or at the Paris police prefecture (the prefecture of the Seine) for Paris, a filing renewed with every change of bylaws or leadership. The mayor or prefect must then pass the contents on to the public prosecutor. The same article reserves the leadership of unions to persons of French nationality enjoying their civil rights, which excludes foreigners from their governing bodies. The law also frames the unions' purpose: Article 3 limits it to the study and defense of economic, industrial, commercial, and agricultural interests, with no mention of any political aim.

## What the Law Does Not Do

The 1884 law does not create the right to strike: that already exists since the Ollivier law of May 25, 1864, which ended the offense of coalition (the crime of workers combining to act collectively) without authorizing permanent organizations. What Waldeck-Rousseau adds is the possibility of organizing outside the moment of conflict alone, with a continuous existence, property limited to what is needed for meetings, a library, and vocational training courses, and the right to sue, which Article 6 reserves to properly constituted unions only. What is born is thus a declared freedom rather than an anonymous one: a union that does not report itself to the administration enjoys none of the rights the law grants it.

This conditionality, largely erased today behind the image of a law of freedom, says something more general about collective freedoms granted by law: they almost always come with a price in visibility, the recognition of a right being paid for, by the person exercising it, with the authority that grants it being able to know who exercises it.

repere.texte: The bill on trade unions is introduced in the Chamber of Deputies on November 22, 1880; it is promulgated only on March 21, 1884, after more than three years of back-and-forth between the Chamber and the Senate.
repere.source: Law of March 21, 1884 on the creation of trade unions, Digithèque of legal and political materials, University of Perpignan

carte.punch: In 1884, unions become free, provided they declare themselves to the mayor
carte.idee: On March 21, 1884, the Waldeck-Rousseau law authorizes the free creation of trade unions and ends 93 years of prohibition inherited from the Le Chapelier law. This freedom remains conditional: each union must file its bylaws at city hall, which passes them to the prosecutor.

quiz.question: Why did the Waldeck-Rousseau law of March 21, 1884 have to create a special rule for unions, rather than simply loosening the ordinary law on associations?
choix: Because the 1834 law required prior government authorization for any association of more than twenty members, and unions had to be expressly exempted from it
Because unions wanted a different tax status from ordinary associations, with a complete tax exemption
Because the Constitution of 1875 reserved the right of association to political parties alone, to the exclusion of any professional grouping
Because the courts refused to hear any case involving more than twenty people gathered in the same profession
quiz.explication: The law of April 18, 1834 subjected any association of more than twenty people to prior authorization, on pain of Articles 291 to 294 of the penal code. Trade unions, often larger, needed an explicit exemption, which Article 1 of the 1884 law provides by expressly setting these provisions aside for them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What must the founders of a union file under Article 4 of the 1884 law?
choix: The union's bylaws and the names of its leaders, at the town hall or, for Paris, at the prefecture of the Seine
A financial deposit equal to one month of dues from all members
An annual activity report sent directly to the Interior Minister
The full list of all their members, including non-unionized sympathizers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 4 requires filing the bylaws and the names of the leaders at the town hall, or at the prefecture of the Seine for Paris, renewed with every change; the other obligations listed do not exist in the law.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What had the Ollivier law of May 25, 1864 already accomplished before the 1884 law?
choix: It had authorized the formation of permanent unions endowed with property
It had given unions the right to sue
It had ended the offense of coalition, without authorizing any permanent professional organization
It had abolished the 1791 Le Chapelier law in its entirety
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1864 Ollivier law abolishes the offense of coalition and thus allows strikes, but creates no permanent structure: it is the 1884 law that adds continuous existence, limited property, and the right to sue.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Whom does the 1884 law exclude from the leadership of a union?
choix: Women, excluded from union voting rights until 1920
Persons who are not of French nationality enjoying their civil rights
Employees under twenty-one, considered minors under civil law
Former convicts of the offense of coalition under the previous regime
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 4 reserves the leadership of unions to persons of French nationality enjoying their civil rights, which excludes foreigners from their governing bodies.
